1.note: God is repeating forms of the verb **Comfort** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Surely comfort my people]

The word **your** is plural here because Yahweh is speaking to the messengers whom he is sending to comfort his people. If your language distinguishes between singular and plural forms of **you**, use the plural form here.

2.note: Here, **the heart of Jerusalem** represents the inner feelings of the people of the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Speak to the inner feelings of the people of Jerusalem]

2.q: דַּבְּר֞וּ עַל־לֵ֤ב יְרֽוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ וְ⁠קִרְא֣וּ אֵלֶ֔י⁠הָ כִּ֤י מָֽלְאָה֙ צְבָאָ֔⁠הּ כִּ֥י נִרְצָ֖ה עֲוֺנָ֑⁠הּ כִּ֤י לָקְחָה֙ מִ⁠יַּ֣ד יְהוָ֔ה כִּפְלַ֖יִם בְּ⁠כָל־חַטֹּאתֶֽי⁠הָ
2.note: The pronouns **her** and **she** refer to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and proclaim to Jerusalem that her service is full, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she, Jerusalem, has received from the hand of Yahweh double for all her sins]

2.q: כִּ֤י מָֽלְאָה֙ צְבָאָ֔⁠הּ כִּ֥י נִרְצָ֖ה עֲוֺנָ֑⁠הּ כִּ֤י
2.note: Yahweh is speaking of the city Jerusalem as if it were a woman who could perform **service** and commit **iniquity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that the people of Jerusalem have completed their service, that their iniquity is pardoned, that]

The expression **is pardoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that I, Yahweh, have pardoned her iniquity]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the wicked things she had done]

Here, **the hand of Yahweh** represents the power and action of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from Yahweh himself]

3.note: Isaiah is using **A voice** to represent the person who is calling out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Someone is calling out]

3.q: ק֣וֹל קוֹרֵ֔א בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֕ר פַּנּ֖וּ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יְהוָ֑ה יַשְּׁרוּ֙ בָּ⁠עֲרָבָ֔ה מְסִלָּ֖ה לֵ⁠אלֹהֵֽי⁠נוּ
3.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Make a road through the wilderness so that Yahweh and our God may come]

Here the speaker is speaking of preparing for Yahweh to come to his people as if people were building and clearing a road for a king to travel on. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make the road ready for Yahweh to come through the wilderness]

4.q: כָּל גֶּיא֙ יִנָּשֵׂ֔א וְ⁠כָל הַ֥ר וְ⁠גִבְעָ֖ה יִשְׁפָּ֑לוּ
4.note: Here the speaker is speaking of preparing for Yahweh to come as if workers needed to level the landscape, raising up low places and bringing down high places so that the road would be smooth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Raise up the valleys and bring down the mountains and hills]

4.q: כָּל גֶּיא֙ יִנָּשֵׂ֔א וְ⁠כָל הַ֥ר וְ⁠גִבְעָ֖ה יִשְׁפָּ֑לוּ
4.note: The speaker is referring to all of the terrain by naming two major components, the low places, **every valley**, and the high places, **every mountain and hill**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let all the land be made level, both the low places and the high places]

The expression **be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let every valley rise]

5.note: The expression **will be revealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the glory of Yahweh will appear]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s glorious presence]
Here, **all flesh** represents all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all people]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

The speaker is using **the mouth of Yahweh** to represent Yahweh himself in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh himself has spoken]

6.note: Here the speaker is speaking of human beings as if they were **grass**, which springs up and then quickly withers. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All flesh is temporary]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the flower of the field** is short-lived and quickly fades, so is **all of its covenant faithfulness**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and all of its covenant faithfulness fades quickly, just as the flower of the field fades]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and all of their faithful keeping of the covenant]
The pronoun **its** refers to all flesh, that is, to all people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and all the covenant faithfulness of the people]

7.note: Here, **the breath of Yahweh** represents the power of Yahweh acting against the grass, like a scorching wind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sends a scorching wind on it]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since]

Here the speaker is speaking of the people as if they were **grass**, which dries up and dies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [surely the people dry up and die like grass]

8.q: יָבֵ֥שׁ חָצִ֖יר נָ֣בֵֽל צִ֑יץ וּ⁠דְבַר אֱלֹהֵ֖י⁠נוּ יָק֥וּם לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
8.note: The speaker uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the grass and flowers, which quickly perish, and the word of God, which lasts forever. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Even though the grass dries up and the flower withers, the word of our God will stand forever]

The speaker is speaking of **the word of our God** as if it were a living thing that could stand forever. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but what our God says will always come true]

Here, **the word of our God** represents what God has spoken and promised. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but what our God has spoken and promised]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the grass and flower that wither and the word of God that endures forever. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [yet the word of our God will stand forever]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **word** that is characterized as belonging to our God, that is, what God himself has spoken. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but what our God has spoken]

9.note: The word **yourself** and the implied “you” in the imperative **Go up** are feminine singular because they refer to the **herald** whom Isaiah is addressing. (That term is feminine, since it is equivalent to **Zion** and **Jerusalem**. That city is being personified as a woman.) For the same reason, the term **your** and the implied “you” in the imperatives **Raise** and **Say** are feminine singular. However, the implied “you” in the imperative **Behold** is masculine plural, since it addresses **the cities of Judah**. Use the appropriate singular or plural and feminine or masculine forms in your translation if your language marks those distinctions.

Isaiah is using these possessive forms to describe a **herald** who is characterized by being the city of **Zion**, that is, **Jerusalem**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Zion, you herald … Jerusalem, you herald]

Here, **your voice** represents the message that the herald is to proclaim. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Proclaim your message strongly]

Here, **the cities of Judah** represents the people who live in those cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people living in the cities of Judah]

10.q: הִנֵּ֨ה אֲדֹנָ֤⁠י יְהוִה֙ בְּ⁠חָזָ֣ק יָב֔וֹא וּ⁠זְרֹע֖⁠וֹ מֹ֣שְׁלָה ל֑⁠וֹ הִנֵּ֤ה שְׂכָר⁠וֹ֙ אִתּ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠פְעֻלָּת֖⁠וֹ לְ⁠פָנָֽי⁠ו
10.note: The speaker is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look, the Lord Yahweh comes with strength, and his arm is ruling for him. And look, his reward is with him, and his recompense is to his face.]

Here, **his arm** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and his great power is ruling for him]

Here, **to his face** represents being in his presence, that is, with him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and his recompense is with him]

11.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a shepherd** lovingly tends and protects his sheep, so Yahweh will care for **his flock**, that is, his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He will care for his people lovingly, just as a shepherd tends his flock]

Here the speaker is speaking of Yahweh’s people as if they were **his flock** of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his people, who are his flock]

Here, **his arm** represents the protective care with which Yahweh holds and shelters his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [With his protective care he will gather the lambs]

12.q: מִֽי מָדַ֨ד בְּ⁠שָׁעֳל֜⁠וֹ מַ֗יִם וְ⁠שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ בַּ⁠זֶּ֣רֶת תִּכֵּ֔ן וְ⁠כָ֥ל בַּ⁠שָּׁלִ֖שׁ עֲפַ֣ר הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ וְ⁠שָׁקַ֤ל בַּ⁠פֶּ֨לֶס֙ הָרִ֔ים וּ⁠גְבָע֖וֹת בְּ⁠מֹאזְנָֽיִם
12.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no human being could do these things that Yahweh alone, the all-powerful Creator, can do. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely no one has measured the waters in his palm or measured the heavens with a span or held the dust of the earth in a triple or weighed the mountains in a scale or the hills in a balance!]

For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates each one as **measured** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here.

By **the waters**, Isaiah means all the waters on the earth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the waters on the earth]

Here, **his palm** represents the small amount that a person can hold or measure in his hand. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in his cupped hand]

A **triple** is a a Hebrew unit of dry measurement for grain or flour which literally means “a third.” If your readers would not be familiar with what a triple is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a measuring bowl] or [a cup]

13.q: מִֽי תִכֵּ֥ן אֶת ר֖וּחַ יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠אִ֥ישׁ עֲצָת֖⁠וֹ יוֹדִיעֶֽ⁠נּוּ
13.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one has comprehended Yahweh’s Spirit or given him advice, since he needs no instruction from anyone. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one has measured the Spirit of Yahweh or, as a man of his counsel, has advised him.]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **man** who is characterized by **counsel**, that is, someone who advises Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or {as} a man who gives counsel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or, as a man who counsels him]

14.q: אֶת מִ֤י נוֹעָץ֙ וַ⁠יְבִינֵ֔⁠הוּ וַֽ⁠יְלַמְּדֵ֖⁠הוּ בְּ⁠אֹ֣רַח מִשְׁפָּ֑ט וַ⁠יְלַמְּדֵ֣⁠הוּ דַ֔עַת וְ⁠דֶ֥רֶךְ תְּבוּנ֖וֹת יוֹדִיעֶֽ⁠נּוּ
14.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one ever counseled or taught Yahweh, because his wisdom and knowledge come from himself alone. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one counseled him, and no one made him understand and taught him in the path of justice and taught him knowledge and made him know the way of understanding.]

The expression **was he counseled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [What person counseled him]

Here the speaker is speaking of acting justly as if it were a **path** that a person walks along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to act justly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [taught him what to know]

Here Isaiah is speaking of how to understand things as if **understanding** were a **way** or path that a person walks along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to understand things]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how to understand]

15.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look! the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and they are regarded like dust on the scales. And look, he lifts the coastlands like fine dust]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a drop from a bucket** is tiny and insignificant compared to all the water, so are **the nations** small and insignificant before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the nations are tiny and insignificant]

Here, **the nations** represents the people who make up those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of those nations]

The point of this comparison is that just as **dust on the scales** is too light to make any difference in weighing, so do **they**, the nations, count for nothing before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they count for nothing before him]

The expression **are regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he regards them like dust on the scales]

Isaiah is using the **coastlands**, the edge of the earth by the sea, to represent the whole earth. This idea is parallel to **the nations** earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the whole world]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fine dust** is light and easy to pick up, so easily can Yahweh lift up **the coastlands**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he easily lifts the coastlands, for they are as light to him as fine dust]

16.q: וּ⁠לְבָנ֕וֹן אֵ֥ין דֵּ֖י בָּעֵ֑ר וְ⁠חַיָּת֔⁠וֹ אֵ֥ין דֵּ֖י עוֹלָֽה
16.note: By **not enough to burn**, Isaiah means that Lebanon, famous for its great forests of massive trees, could not supply the firewood needed for a suitable sacrifice to Yahweh. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [All the wood of Lebanon would not be enough, nor would all of Lebanon’s animals be enough for a proper burnt offering for Yahweh]

17.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **nought** is nothing at all, so are **all of the nations** of no significance before Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [All of the nations are like nought before him, meaning they have no significance at all]

The expression **are regarded by him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he regards them]

Isaiah says that the nations are **less than nothing and emptiness** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [as completely worthless and insignificant]

18.q: וְ⁠אֶל מִ֖י תְּדַמְּי֣וּ⁠ן אֵ֑ל וּ⁠מַה דְּמ֖וּת תַּ֥עַרְכוּ לֽ⁠וֹ
18.note: Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So there is no one to whom you can liken God, and no likeness you can compare to him!]

The word **you** is plural here and in verses 21 and 26 because Isaiah is addressing the cities of Judah, whom he named in verse 9. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

19.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Would you compare him to an idol]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize his point. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You would not compare God to an idol!]

20.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contribution**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The person who cannot afford to contribute]

The expression **will not be moved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [an idol that will not topple]

21.q: הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא תֵֽדְעוּ֙ הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא תִשְׁמָ֔עוּ הֲ⁠ל֛וֹא הֻגַּ֥ד מֵ⁠רֹ֖אשׁ לָ⁠כֶ֑ם הֲ⁠לוֹא֙ הֲבִ֣ינֹתֶ֔ם מוֹסְד֖וֹת הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
21.note: Isaiah is using the question form to rebuke his listeners and to emphasize that they certainly should know these truths about God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You do know! You have heard! It has been declared to you from the beginning! You have understood {from} the foundations of the earth!]

The expression **been declared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Has no one declared it to you]

22.note: Here the speaker is speaking of Yahweh’s ruling over the world as if he were **sitting** enthroned above the circle of the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who rules over the whole earth from above]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grasshoppers** are tiny and insignificant, so do **its dwellers** appear small and insignificant to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and its dwellers appear tiny and insignificant to him]
The pronoun **its** refers to the earth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the dwellers of the earth]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a curtain** is easily stretched out, so easily did Yahweh spread out **the heavens**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the one stretching out the heavens as easily as someone stretches out a curtain]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a tent** is stretched out to make a place to dwell, so did Yahweh spread out **the heavens** over the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he spreads them out to make a place to dwell in, just as a tent is spread out]

23.q: הַ⁠נּוֹתֵ֥ן רוֹזְנִ֖ים לְ⁠אָ֑יִן שֹׁ֥פְטֵי אֶ֖רֶץ כַּ⁠תֹּ֥הוּ עָשָֽׂה
23.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **emptiness** has no substance, so does Yahweh make **the judges of the earth** count for nothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the one making princes into nothing; he makes the judges of the earth to have no substance]

Here the speaker is speaking of Yahweh’s removing rulers from power as if he reduced them to **nothing**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who makes princes powerless; he makes the judges of]

24.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the princes and judges mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Indeed, the princes and judges are not planted]

24.q: בַּל נִטָּ֗עוּ אַ֚ף בַּל זֹרָ֔עוּ אַ֛ף בַּל שֹׁרֵ֥שׁ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ גִּזְעָ֑⁠ם
24.note: Here the speaker is speaking of rulers as if they were freshly planted seedlings that have barely taken root and can be easily destroyed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are barely established; indeed, they are not secure; indeed, they have no firm foundation in the earth]

The expression **are not planted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they did not get planted]

The expression **are not sown** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one has sown them]

The speaker speaks of the rulers as if they were plants on which Yahweh **blows** so that **they dry up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he breathes on them and they perish]

The point of this comparison is that just as **straw** is light and easily blown away, so easily does **a whirlwind** sweep the rulers away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and a whirlwind carries them away as easily as it carries away straw]

24.q: אַ֣ף בַּל־נִטָּ֗עוּ אַ֚ף בַּל־זֹרָ֔עוּ אַ֛ף בַּל־שֹׁרֵ֥שׁ בָּ⁠אָ֖רֶץ גִּזְעָ֑⁠ם
24.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Truly, those people are not securely rooted]

25.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that there is no one to whom he can be compared and no one who is equal to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So there is no one to whom you can liken me or who is equal to me.]

26.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that it was God who created the stars. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God is the one who created these!]

Here the speaker is speaking of the stars as if they were **their army** that Yahweh musters and leads out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one bringing out all the stars by number]
The pronoun **their** refers to the stars. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the stars’ army]

The speaker is speaking of the stars as if they were living beings that each have a name by which Yahweh calls **all of them**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he calls each one of them as if it has a name]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe **greatness** that is characterized by **might**, that is, his great might. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because he is so mighty]

The expression **is not missing** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [not one of them fails to come]

27.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people of Israel for complaining that he does not see or care about their situation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Jacob, Israel, you should not say]

The names **Jacob** and **Israel** here refer to the people of Israel, who were descended from the man Jacob, who was also called Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Why do you say, O people of Jacob, and speak, O people of Israel]

Here the speaker is speaking of his life and circumstances as if they were a **way** or road that he was traveling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My situation is hidden from Yahweh]

The expression **is hidden** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh does not know my way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and my God does not treat me justly”]

28.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that the people certainly should know and have heard these truths about God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Surely you know! Surely you have heard!]
See how you translated the term “Or” in 10:9. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

The speaker is using the possessive form to describe a **God** who is characterized by **eternity**, that is, the God who exists forever. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The God who lives forever]

Here the speaker is speaking of the most distant regions of the world as if they were the **ends of the earth**, the places where the earth comes to an end. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the farthest parts of the earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **understanding**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [No one can search all that he understands]

29.note: The speaker is using the adjective **tired** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to those who are tired]

30.q: וְ⁠יִֽעֲפ֥וּ נְעָרִ֖ים וְ⁠יִגָ֑עוּ וּ⁠בַחוּרִ֖ים כָּשׁ֥וֹל יִכָּשֵֽׁלוּ
30.note: The speaker is referring to all of the strongest people by naming two major components, **youths** and **young men**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Even the strongest people tire and become weary, and they stumble and fall]

31.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **eagles** soar high on their wings without growing tired, so will those who wait for Yahweh **ascend** with renewed strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They will ascend on wings like eagles, never growing weary]

31.q: יָר֨וּצוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יִיגָ֔עוּ יֵלְכ֖וּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יִיעָֽפוּ
31.note: The speaker is referring to all of their activity by naming two major components, **run** and **walk**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They will do all kinds of activities and not grow tired]
